extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, researchers, peer reviewers, and science journalists interested in publication and research integrity
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and evaluating standards and failures related to integrity, authorship, citation accuracy, data quality, conflicts of interest, and editorial corrections in biomedical journal publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabricated / hallucinated citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers must not reference works that do not exist; fabricated citations (hallucinated references) are a form of invalid scholarship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis found a sharp increase in papers referencing nonexistent articles, with AI tools implicated; researchers used AI to distinguish genuine fabrications from formatting discrepancies such as informally abbreviated titles. Journals, reviewers, and authors should verify reference existence and accuracy; AI can both produce and help detect hallucinated references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification of citations (citation integrity)
rubrics_metrics.description: References in manuscripts should be checked for existence, correct metadata, and accurate attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formatting discrepancies (e.g., abbreviated titles) must be distinguished from true fabrications. The rise of AI writing tools increases risk of invalid or imagined references, so extra verification by authors, reviewers, and editors is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of conflicts of interest (COI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must disclose relevant financial or professional ties that could bias the work; undisclosed ties can justify retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A half-century-old unsigned commentary was retracted after discovering the author was a paid consultant to industry; undisclosed industry ties that materially affect the work’s trustworthiness are grounds for corrective action by journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty about prior publication / originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must honestly represent whether material has been published previously and must not misrepresent originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misrepresenting prior publication or claiming novelty when the work was already published can lead to retraction, as when authors misled a journal about prior publication of a case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data integrity and accuracy (no undisclosed data errors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Data and analyses must be accurate; discovered errors that materially affect results require correction, expression of concern, retraction, or replacement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals may flag papers with expressions of concern and investigate when readers identify data errors. Authors who discover errors are expected to contact the journal promptly; substantial errors that change numbers or conclusions may prompt retraction and replacement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of expressions of concern and investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should use formal notices (e.g., expressions of concern) to alert readers while investigating credible allegations about a paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Lancet flagged a paper with an expression of concern after a reader brought 'data errors' to light and after external investigative reporting raised questions. Expressions of concern are an intermediate editorial step while investigations proceed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt author-initiated correction and editor response
rubrics_metrics.description: When errors are identified (by authors, readers, or editors), authors should report them and journals should correct the record in a timely and transparent way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: authors contacted the journal immediately after finding errors that changed 'all numbers' and the journal retracted and replaced the paper. Failure to correct inaccuracies undermines trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction, retraction, and replace policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals must correct the scholarly record by issuing corrections, retracting faulty items, or retracting-and-replacing when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals have retracted pieces (including news stories) and replaced them after removing information deemed inaccurate; retraction may be applied decades later if undisclosed conflicts or misrepresentations are discovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial responsibility to publish responses and corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and journals should consider publishing authors' or critics' responses and corrections when substantive inaccuracies or critiques are raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refusal by journals or platforms to publish responses or make requested corrections has been criticized; transparent handling of critiques and corrections is an editorial duty for maintaining trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of citation-metric manipulation (self-citation and gaming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals and authors should not manipulate citation practices to artificially inflate metrics such as impact factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarivate suppressed journals for self-citation and warned others; responsible citation practices and editorial policies should guard against gaming bibliometric indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation of allegations raised by external reporting or readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should investigate credible allegations arising from investigative journalism or reader reports that call into question a paper's validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations (including editorial expressions of concern or retractions) have followed external investigations and reader-identified problems; journals should take such external evidence seriously and act transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutiny of citations to retracted or fraudulent work
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations to retracted or fraudulent papers should be examined to understand why they persist in the literature and whether they propagate false claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work examining citations to the Wakefield paper sought to characterize why a retracted fraudulent article continued to be cited; reviewers and editors should consider context when encountering citations to retracted literature.
